title: Knowledge Check 6: Lessons 41-46
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 41-46 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Experience Cloud Architecture: Sites, Communities, Licensing, and Sharing”, a manufacturer is building a brand new, read-mostly partner portal that the team fully controls. Which framework fits, and what does the choice force you to design around?
options: Aura, because it applies component changes immediately and needs no republish step.
LWR, because it pre-compiles and caches static content at publish time, and you design around the republish cadence and object-specific record pages.
Visualforce, because it gives the most control over rendering for external users.
LWR, because it restores the generic record detail page that Aura templates lacked.
questions.explanation: LWR is the strategic direction for a new build and the performance is real, and the trade is that component changes need a republish and record components are only usable on object-specific pages.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Guest users consume external licenses, so a public knowledge base has to be sized like any other external audience.
Community licenses attach to a site rather than to a user, so an unused license cannot be reassigned across sites.
The plain Customer Community license carries roles and standard sharing rules, which is why it suits partners as well as consumers.
Internal licenses are not suited to securing an external-facing portal, because an internal license grants far more capability than an outsider should ever hold.
questions.explanation: Licenses attach to users rather than pages, guests cost nothing because no licensed user is behind the session, and putting community users on internal licenses is exactly how a portal leaks.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A sharing set grants access through the account or contact relationship and does not roll up through the role hierarchy, so it does not extend access to a user’s superiors.
Sharing sets are available only on the Partner Community license, which is why partner portals need role-based sharing.
The guest user profile is safe to leave permissive because guests are unauthenticated and therefore see nothing by default.
An external user’s access is governed by the site’s framework alone, not by the license they hold or by the org’s sharing model.
questions.explanation: The sharing set is keyed to the user’s own account or contact and deliberately does not roll up the hierarchy, so role-based visibility is what the Plus and Partner tiers add.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Lightning Web Components Architecture: Composition, Wire Service, and Data Services”, a child component dispatches a CustomEvent that a grandparent utility panel must hear. What event configuration is required?
options: bubbles: true only, because composed is implied once a shadow root exists.
bubbles: true and composed: true, because the event has to bubble up and cross a shadow boundary.
composed: true only, because events bubble by default.
Neither, because Lightning web components use only the capture phase for dispatch and listening.
questions.explanation: bubbles defaults to false and composed defaults to false, so a direct parent needs bubbles and only an event that must cross a shadow root adds composed.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: After an imperative write, the wired reads on the same screen need refreshApex, because the cache and the write otherwise disagree and the screen keeps showing stale data.
A write should be wired with cacheable=true so the framework re-provisions the record automatically once it changes.
Data flows from child to parent through @api attributes, and consequences flow back down through events.
Lightning Data Service is a server-side cache, so a component that changes a record leaves every other component on the page unaware.
questions.explanation: Writes are inherently imperative because cacheable methods cannot mutate data, so a wired read on the same screen has to be refreshed explicitly after the write resolves.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Subclassing components in JavaScript is the recommended way to share logic between two components.
Setting composed: true by default keeps a component tree easy to reason about.
Lightning Data Service is built on User Interface API, which respects CRUD, field-level security, and sharing, so a component gets the org’s security model with no extra code on your side.
A method used with @wire must be cacheable in order to compile, and a cacheable method may perform DML as long as its result is cached.
questions.explanation: LDS and the wire adapters sit on UI API, which returns data and metadata matching the org’s layout and enforces object permissions, FLS, and sharing for the running user.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Lightning Performance: Caching, Static Resources, and What Slows Users Down”, an org created before Winter ’19 has never had Session Settings opened, and the team wants the cheapest real wins first. Which two changes cost nothing and can be made today?
options: Enable the CDN for the Lightning component framework after IT allowlists static.lightning.force.com, and confirm secure and persistent browser caching is enabled.
Move the chart library into a static resource, and cap the related list to the columns on screen.
Replace the wired Apex calls with Lightning Data Service adapters, and delete the components nobody uses.
Republish the site, and convert every component on the layout to lazy instantiation.
questions.explanation: Both are session settings, both are disabled by default only in older orgs, and together they address framework delivery and repeat-visit reloads before any code changes.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Disabling secure browser caching is a safe way to make component changes appear immediately, and it should be left off afterward.
The CDN distributes your org’s record data and metadata as well as the framework files, which changes where records are served from.
A loadScript call in renderedCallback without a first-render guard re-requests the library on every re-render, so the library belongs in a static resource with Public cache control, loaded once.
Hiding a heavy region with CSS is preferable to conditional rendering, because the element and its listeners are already in the DOM.
questions.explanation: Third-party libraries should be served from a static resource with Public cache control and loaded once on the render that needs them, and conditional rendering beats CSS hiding because it keeps the tree from being built at all.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Experienced page time is measured on the server, so network conditions and device power cannot explain two users seeing different load times.
Server-side selectivity and indexing are the first thing to investigate when a Lightning page feels slow to users.
A wired Apex method that is not cacheable still benefits from the client cache, so the annotation has no performance effect.
Two users in the same org on the same page can legitimately see different experienced page time, because network and device set a floor that no org configuration controls.
questions.explanation: Network, device, browser, and configuration set the floor, and only the last is yours, which is why the server-side work comes after confirming the org-level caches are switched on.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Security Review: OWASP for Apex, SOQL Injection, and Enforcing CRUD and FLS”, a class declares with sharing and builds dynamic SOQL by concatenating a user-supplied field name and a user-supplied WHERE value. What does with sharing actually do here?
options: It enforces record-level sharing only, so it neither stops the field name injection nor enforces CRUD and FLS.
It blocks both injections, because sharing prevents a user from querying fields their profile hides.
It forces the class to use WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED, which the platform adds to the query automatically.
It enforces CRUD and FLS but leaves record visibility to the org-wide default.
questions.explanation: Object permissions, field-level security, and sharing are three separate layers, and the sharing keyword only ever enforces the third one.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: String.escapeSingleQuotes closes both the value case and the field name case, which makes it the general fix.
A bind variable in the WHERE clause also protects a field name that the user supplied.
Because a bind variable treats a value as data, also escaping that value with escapeSingleQuotes inside the bind improves safety.
A bind variable cannot protect a field or object name, because a name is syntax rather than a value, so user-supplied names must be compared against an allowlist.
questions.explanation: Bind variables and queryWithBinds close value injection, an allowlist closes name injection, escaping is a narrow fallback for quoted literals, and typecasting closes the numeric case.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: WITH USER_MODE raises on missing access, which makes it the graceful-degradation option for records arriving from an external payload.

Security.stripInaccessible removes the fields the running user cannot access and returns the records in an SObjectAccessDecision, so the caller has to check getRemovedFields or getModifiedIndexes rather than ignore the result.
WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED is the modern replacement for WITH USER_MODE at API version 67.0 and later.
Apex tests prove security because they run as the user the component renders for.
questions.explanation: stripInaccessible strips rather than raises, which is why its return value has to be inspected; tests run as a broadly permissioned user, so a passing suite proves the code path, not the restriction.

questions.question: Per the lesson, a customer-facing support agent can read Case, Account, Contact, Knowledge, and Opportunity, and it holds an email tool that sends to any address the model provides. An indirect prompt injection in a support message tells the agent to email the top ten opportunities to an external address, and the agent complies. Which change removes the highest-value single slice of the blast radius?
options: Adding a longer and stricter system prompt that instructs the model to ignore instructions inside retrieved content.
Removing the agent user's read access to Opportunity, so the identity cannot reach the data the injection tried to exfiltrate.
Enabling input filtering on the support channel so hostile messages are blocked before the model reads them.
Switching the email tool to send only to addresses the model suggests, so the recipient is always derived from model output.
questions.explanation: The identity caps everything the agent can reach regardless of what the model is tricked into doing. Removing Opportunity access is least privilege on the identity, and the lesson calls it the highest-value single fix because an injection cannot exfiltrate data the identity cannot reach.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on tool permissions?
options: A read-only tool on sensitive data is harmless, because reading cannot change state.
Tool scoping is a one-time decision made at deployment, and later agent actions do not change it.
Every tool is both a capability and an attack surface, so the tool set should stay minimal and each tool's parameter space should be bounded, with human approval on high-impact actions.
The security of an agent is determined by the model's refusal policy, not by the tools it holds.
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the model is not the dangerous part; the tools are. A read tool is still half of an exfiltration, tool scope has to be sized per task and rechecked as actions change, and high-impact actions belong behind a human gate.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what does the concept of least agency add beyond least privilege?
options: It requires every agent to run with the broadest possible autonomy so it can handle unexpected requests.
It restricts the identity's object and field access to the minimum the task needs, and nothing more.
It replaces the agent user with the requesting human's identity in every deployment, including customer-facing agents.

It extends least privilege to the autonomy itself, granting the minimum tool access, credential scope, and self-directed behavior the task needs, because unnecessary autonomy is its own attack surface.
questions.explanation: OWASP introduces least agency as the agentic extension of least privilege: minimum autonomy, minimum tool access, and minimum credential scope, with unnecessary autonomy treated as an expansion of the attack surface rather than added capability.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Multi-Org Architecture: When to Split, and Org-to-Org Integration Patterns”, which situation is a legitimate structural reason to split, and which reason does it replace?
options: A regulatory or compliance walled-garden requirement, which replaces a slow request backlog as a reason to give a line of business its own org.
The lines of business wanting their own space, which is met with a center of excellence, delegated administration, and tiered data architecture instead of a split.
A regulatory or compliance walled-garden requirement that sharing alone cannot satisfy, because the requirement is structural isolation and reviewability, not record visibility.
A desire for a faster-paced release cycle, which a second org delivers with no added integration cost.
questions.explanation: The legitimate split is the one where the wall itself is the requirement, giving a compliance burden its own isolated org and reviewable audit trail, which a sharing model controls visibility but cannot deliver.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Salesforce Connect with the cross-org adapter connects directly to another org’s data over the standard REST API without an intermediary web service, so a spoke can read hub master data with the hub’s permissions enforced.
Salesforce Connect’s cross-org adapter requires a middleware web service between the two orgs, which is why hub-and-spoke needs MuleSoft for every read path.
Platform events cross an org boundary on their own, so no relay is needed for an event published in one org to reach subscribers in another.
Salesforce-to-Salesforce is the recommended modern tool for new org-to-org integrations, because it is the only protocol that links records across two orgs.
questions.explanation: The cross-org adapter uses the platform’s REST API directly between the two orgs with no intermediary, and platform events stay org-scoped, so cross-org event delivery needs a relay bridge.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A multi-org estate shares one transaction across the boundary, so an update reflected in both orgs is atomic by design.
Duplicating canonical reference data into a spoke so it can change locally is a free way to gain autonomy without reconciling two sources of truth.

The two orgs do not share a transaction, so a cross-org integration is still an integration and needs the same idempotency, retry, and testing discipline as any external system, tolerating eventual consistency.
A single user who needs access to two orgs still consumes a single license, because Salesforce licenses a person, not an org.
questions.explanation: Neither org can participate in a transaction the other starts, so the design must tolerate a disagreement window; a user in two orgs consumes a license in each, and duplicated canonical data is a standing reconciliation obligation.
